doc.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004

chapter: Teaching, tradition and the banjo's roots
title: How new tunes are taught to the band by ear
summary: The band learns songs by playing them for each other, letting Future Man and Victor find their own parts, as with the funk backbeat on 'Sinister Minister'. Time on stage helps; studio prep makes Fleck pushier.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: When you bring a tune to the band, or the other fellows, does it come notated or do you just kind of get together and —
No. We just play it for each other.

A lot of times we don’t even do that. A lot of times it’ll just be a sound check. Like today we’ll get on stage, right now we’re not really working on anything new because we’ve only got a few days left of the trip, but if I’ve got something I’ve been working on I might just start playing it. And then sometimes Future Man will be playing a beat and he’ll fall in and he’ll find it and then I might say, “oh well there’s a new one here.” And he’ll go, oh. But for a long time I won’t even say that because I’ll just see what he does.

And sometimes he’ll just sort of thread through it, and then Victor will start playing and if I’m behaving I won’t even tell them what the notes are. But sometimes I can’t help myself and I go oh, there’s really an F sharp right there. Because a lot of times he’ll just sort of play simply just until he sort of figures it out. Because I want him to harmonize it himself and find something that I wouldn’t have naturally heard. Once I tell him what I’m hearing he’s going to play it that way from then on, so then he’ll be trapped by that structure. But sometimes he’s found things that I never would have thought of. And Future Man same thing. “Sinister Minister” was supposed to be a Brazilian tune. But when I started playing it for Future Man he put that funk backbeat on it and it was like, if I had told him it was a Brazilian tune it would have never been what it ended up being. So I’ve tried to keep that in mind. And some songs you just have to tell a person it’s a G sharp diminished chord, or it’s not a minor chord it’s a half diminished or it’s — but their ears are so good.
That’s a great system. I mean again I think it takes — it’s about ego.

Yeah but also it’s about like having time on stage everyday. The fact that we play so many gigs that we can sort of work our way into a song in a real kind of easygoing way, there’s no big hurry. Except like when we’re trying to make a record then there’s a pressure and then I get a little more testy and picky, because I’m pushing everybody and I’m trying to shape everybody into this tight thing so that when we get in the studio we can just nail it. And I think that’s hard to be around. When we’re getting ready to record I think I’m harder to be around. But they all know me, you know, they know where I’m coming from and they know it’ll be over and we’ll come out with something good and that they’ll have a lot of input and it’ll be ours together I think. But I like to recognize it because I’m trying not to beat anybody up. Through the process I’m trying to get better at not —
